claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was an early Christian theologian and ascetic active in the early decades of the third century, born c. 185 and died c. 253.
Origen was later condemned as a heretic.
Origen's exegetical works cover most of the New Testament, including multiple-volume commentaries on Matthew, John and Romans, homilies on Luke, Acts and Hebrews and, possibly, scholia on Revelation.
Most of Origen's commentaries have not survived and portions are only known through translations or discoveries such as the Tura papyri.
Catena manuscripts can be valuable as a source of otherwise lost extracts from Origen's writings.

Origen was one of the most prolific writers in late antiquity, producing roughly 2,000 treatises in multiple branches of theology, including textual criticism, biblical exegesis and hermeneutics, homiletics, and spirituality.
Origen was one of the most influential and controversial figures in early Christian theology, apologetics, and asceticism.

Origen was the first Christian textual critic, and his writings are crucial for tracking New Testament textual variants because he quotes liberally from scripture and comments on variants already existing at the time of his writing.
Origen's Commentary on Matthew was written about the same time as the Contra Celsum, when Origen was over sixty years of age, probably assigned to the period 246-248.

Of the twenty-five books into which the Commentary on Matthew was divided, the first nine are mostly lost; books 10-17 are extant in Greek, and the greater part of the remaining books survives in a Latin version.
